terms.comment: From animum advertere, “turn the mind to”, which Cato and Cicero still write as two words (Agr. 1.2; Tusc. 5.65). With an accusative, an accusative and infinitive (notice that …) or a question (Lewis & Short). What one notices by ear or by touch is often sentīre (see feel).

phrases.latin: animadvertī pauperem mendīcum, jam, crēdō, saturum, jocantem atque laetantem
phrases.english: I noticed a poor beggar, already full, I suppose, joking and cheerful

phrases.latin: ut in fidibus aut tībiīs, quamvīs paulum discrepent, tamen id ā sciente animadvertī solet
phrases.english: as with strings or pipes: however slightly they are out of tune, an expert still notices it

phrases.latin: ego autem cum omnia conlūstrārem oculīs … animum advertī columellam nōn multum ē dūmīs ēminentem
phrases.english: as I was looking all around … I noticed a little column standing a short way out of the brambles

sources: Lewis & Short: animadverto · Lewis & Short: conspicio
